item.title: Tibet floods: China is keeping tight control over the narrative by deleting videos, censoring news
item.description: It reflects a longstanding tendency in Chinese media to avoid material that could cause social instability or public panic.
item.content:encoded:
As rescue efforts have continued on both sides of the border following the devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet, a fight over how the disaster is being reported has been growing in intensity on social media.

The dispute centres on the claims and counterclaims following a story by the BBC’s China correspondent, Laura Bicker, about how China is censoring videos of the floods.

Bicker said videos of the landslide and flood surge sweeping through Gyirong Port on the border was scrubbed from the internet, in part, because Beijing fears instability in the politically sensitive region of Tibet.

Some social media users, however, have posted screenshots of the footage used by the BBC, pointing out it had actually been shown in the Chinese media. One Chinese journalist put it bluntly: “Never seen the BBC spread rumours so blatantly”.

Another X user said the “middle ground often gets lost” in heated debates like this over Chinese censorship.

The Chinese government has long complained about what it sees as Western media “bias” in reporting on Tibet. Its supporters seem to have doubled down on this narrative this week on social media, zeroing in on the BBC.

item.title: Ram temple trust appoints retired Air Marshal Jeetendra Mishra as first CEO
item.description: The ex-officer, who served as Western Air Command chief during Operation Sindoor, was appointed to the post amid allegations of theft of temple donations.
item.content:encoded:
The trust that administers the Ram temple in Ayodhya on Wednesday named retired Air Marshal Jeetendra Mishra as its first chief executive officer.

Jeetendra Mishra commanded the Air Force’s Western Air Command during Operation Sindoor, the military operation against Pakistan-based terrorist bases launched after the Pahalgam terror attack. He was among seven military officers awarded the Sarvottam Yudh Seva Medal for their roles in the operation.

The Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust also appointed three new members: Mahesh Bhagchandka, Madan Mohan Pandey and Nirmala Yadav. The appointments came against the backdrop of a controversy about the alleged embezzlement of donations at the Ram temple.

The three new appointments followed the resignation of Vishwa Hindu Parishad leader Champat Rai and trustee Anil Mishra, who stepped down after the allegations emerged. The third vacancy was created by the death of Vimlendra Pratap Mishra, a member of Ayodhya’s erstwhile royal family, on August 23.

item.title: Horror fiction: A dentist in 1990s Lahore begins to notice strange patterns in his patients
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Haunting of Dr Shamsi: And Other Unsettling Tales’, by Ayesha Muzaffar.
item.content:encoded:
Rahim and Salman were part of a group of six. There were others – Jahangir, Aamir, Farooq, and Zulfi. They weren’t the closest of friends, not the kind who would stand by each other through thick and thin, but there was happiness to their togetherness – shared meals, half-finished jokes, casual arguments – that Rahim had come to hold dear. He was simply Rahim now – a boy among boys, laughing like he had always belonged.

One weekend night, a strike broke out among the locals. It wasn’t the first time unrest had rippled through the city, but this one was different. Sirens in the distance. Fires whispered about but never confirmed. It was serious enough for the warden to issue an unusual order: all students were to sleep in groups of ten in the main hall. Safety in numbers, they were told. They carried their mattresses across the corridors, through vast halls that smelled of damp carpets. item.title: How a ‘super El Niño’ could make India’s monsoon drier – yet more dangerous
item.description: It could create an apparently contradictory situation: less rain over the season as a whole, but heavier rain when it does rain.
item.content:encoded:
India is currently in the middle of its summer monsoon, but this year’s rainfall presents an interesting paradox. Much of the country has received less rain than usual so far, yet has still been hit by severe floods and landslides. In Kerala, for example, devastating floods occurred despite the overall monsoon rainfall remaining well below average.

A weaker monsoon does not necessarily mean an absence of extreme rainfall. Rainfall can be highly uneven, with long dry spells broken by intense cloudbursts that cause flooding and landslides. This year’s experience in Kerala illustrates the apparent contradiction: a season that is dry overall can still produce devastating rainfall.

Amid this highly uneven monsoon, attention is also turning to something happening thousands of kilometres away in the tropical Pacific Ocean: El Niño.

It is well established that El Niño years, when certain parts of the Pacific are warmer than usual, are often associated with weaker Indian monsoon rainfall. Meanwhile La Niña – the opposite state to El Niño – tends to favour wetter conditions. This year, El Niño conditions have developed rapidly in the Pacific, with forecasts suggesting it could become exceptionally strong.

They described the Hindutva organisation as “an authoritarian and militarist group which drew explicit inspiration from European fascism”.

In their letter on Wednesday, they also urged the mayor to confirm that no mayoral representative would attend any RSS-linked event.

The RSS is the parent organisation of the Bharatiya Janata Party.

Bhagwat is expected to arrive in the United Kingdom on Wednesday after having visited the United States and Canada.

The groups took note of allegations of the involvement of RSS-affiliated groups in the 2002 Gujarat riots, and mentioned that a report by the British High Commission from that time had described the riots as having “all the hallmarks of ethnic cleansing”.

The 2002 riots had led to a de facto travel ban on BJP leader and Prime Minister Narendra Modi in the UK. It was lifted in 2012.

item.description: The action against Aakriti Chaudhary was based on a ‘concocted story’, the bench held, ordering the UP government to pay Rs 5 lakh compensation to her.
item.content:encoded:
The Allahabad High Court quashed the preventive detention under the National Security Act of a 25-year-old Delhi University graduate who has been in jail for nearly five months in connection with the workers’ protest in Noida in April, reported Bar and Bench on Wednesday.

The Act allows for long periods of detention without trial up to a year.

On Tuesday, a bench of Justices Atul Sreedharan and Achal Sachdev held that Aakriti Chaudhary was detained based on a “concocted story” by the Uttar Pradesh government, reported Live Law.

The bench also directed the Noida authorities to pay a compensation of Rs 5 lakh to Chaudhary, Bar and Bench quoted advocate Charlie Prakash as saying.

Chaudhary will remain in jail as she is yet to secure bail in other cases registered in connection with the protests, reported the legal news outlet.

The demonstration had turned violent, with videos widely shared on social media showing some protesters throwing stones and vandalising property.

Gandhi’s lawyer Milind Pawar had asked Satyaki Savarkar what about the Congress leader’s speech had he found defamatory.

item.title: This book explains why cricket’s Women’s Premier League is influential and here to stay
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Miracle Women: Guts to Glory ... Their Ascent, Their Story’, by Swayam Ganguly.
item.content:encoded:
The inaugural season of the Women’s Premier League or the WPL began in 2023 and was organised by the BCCI. Named and modelled after its famous big brother the IPL (Indian Premier League), it transformed women’s cricket in India forever. Today, it has quickly become the world’s premier franchise-based T20 cricket league. The tournament features five teams: Mumbai Indians, Royal Challengers Bengaluru, Delhi Capitals, Gujarat Giants and UP Warriorz.

The inaugural edition of the WPL in 2023 was won by the Mumbai Indians, led by captain Harmanpreet Kaur, who defeated the Delhi Capitals, led by Meg Lanning, in the final by seven wickets. A fun fact is that the Delhi Capitals have reached all the finals in the history of the WPL, only to lose in all of them.

item.title: SC seeks Centre, EC views on introducing ‘totalisers’ to count votes in clusters
item.description: The petitioners in the case have argued that such a system could reduce the chances of post-poll violence.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday asked the Union government to submit its views on introducing a totaliser system to count votes recorded in a cluster of electronic voting machines, reported Live Law.

At present, votes cast in elections are counted booth-wise. A totaliser would allow votes recorded in multiple machines to be counted together. This can make it difficult to determine how any particular booth voted.

The petitioners in the case have argued that introducing a totaliser system can prevent a candidate or a political party from knowing how much support they received at a particular booth, thereby reducing the chances of post-poll violence, reported Live Law.

They have sought that election results be declared at the parliamentary constituency level, instead of disclosing booth-wise figures separately.

On Tuesday, a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana asked the Union government to state if there were hurdles in introducing the system and whether it could have any adverse effects, reported Live Law.

The bench also asked the Election Commission to submit its proposal on the matter to the government.

During the hearing, Kant asked if there was a need for the totaliser system, saying that the booth-wise counting process allows discrepancies or tampering to be detected.

They were also told that vehicle tracking devices on buses should be functional at all times.

The directions came days after a driver and a conductor raped a 17-year-old girl inside a moving sleeper bus.

The crime took place on August 4, while the bus travelled nearly 47 km from Greater Noida to Old Delhi’s Kashmere Gate. The persons accused in the matter, 39-year-old bus driver Kuldeep and 26-year-old conductor Sandeep, have been arrested.

The bus had curtains around its berth, which prevented persons who were outside from seeing what was happening inside the vehicle, The Hindu quoted unidentified police officers as saying.

item.title: More Indian students are abandoning higher education as degrees no longer seem worth the cost
item.description: Political control over educational institutes has lowered the value of academic degrees, which no longer seem worth the cost and time.
item.content:encoded:
While the youth protests were underway at the Jantar Mantar in the first week of July, the Central government published two crucial reports on higher education enrollment: the All India Survey on Higher Education for 2022-’23 and 2023-’24.

The findings were alarming. For the first time since 2011, there has been a decline in the number of Indian students pursuing undergraduate degrees. In 2023-’24, undergraduate enrolment decreased by 93,321 students compared with the previous academic year, representing a decline of 0.29%. This decline at national level might look small. But for a developing country like India enrollments for higher education are supposed to grow fast.

Maharashtra was among the states with the sharpest declines: 5% of Class 12 students here did not enroll in the undergraduate enrollment. This means that nearly 200,000 fewer young people in the state opted for degree programmes compared to the previous year. The number dropped from 35,04,046 in 2023-’24 from 36,88,956 in 2022-’23.

Sanjeev Sanyal, a member of the Prime Minister’s Economic Advisory Council, in an interview to India Today on Tuesday defended the Union government’s change in the methodology for calculating the gross domestic product amid Opposition’s allegations of data manipulation.

“No serious economist is looking at this data and saying that it is not credible,” Sanyal said.

The data released by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation on Monday showed that India’s economy grew 7.8% year-on-year in the April-June quarter, higher than the Reserve Bank of India’s 7% forecast.

Sanyal said that there had been a problem with the methodology to calculate GDP until the base year was updated last year.

The base year is updated at the beginning of each decade, he told the news channel. However, it could not be revised at the start of this decade as the Covid-19 pandemic did not reflect normal economic conditions, he said.

“We had to wait till 2024 before we could get a typical year which we could use as base year,” he added.

item.description: The eight-episode series on JioHotstar stars Lola Petticrew, Emmy Rossum and Quincy Tyler Bernstine.
item.content:encoded:
Furious will go down as one of the definitive explorations of the depraved culture that nurtured predators like Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell. Epstein’s death in prison in 2019, attributed to a suspicious suicide, denied closure to the survivors of his decades-long sex trafficking racket.

Furious captures the seething anger over obstructed justice but does something else too: it shatters perceptions of the ideal victim, presenting instead women who are dark, manipulative, violent and yet wholly worthy of empathy.

The Hulu series, available in India on JioHotstar, aired the last of eight episodes on Monday. Created by Elizabeth Merriweather and co-written by her, Furious is baggily based on Bob Rafelson’s stylish erotic thriller Black Widow (1987).

Black Widow revolves around Catherine, a serial killer who targets wealthy marks, and Alex, the US government official who hunts her down. Catherine is also the name of the young woman in Furious who is luring and then killing off rich, older men. The contempt for women like Catherine, which paradoxically makes her task easier, is captured in the pithy line, one of many memorable pieces of dialogue: “I don’t even remember this girl.”

item.title: Mankind destroyed whatever was gifted as life: Tagore’s lament for the environment 87 years ago
item.description: The Nobel Laureate initiated a tree planting festival at Sriniketan on September 2, 1938 when he gave a prescient address, translated into English here.
item.content:encoded:
About a century ago, long before environmental degradation became the crisis of our times, Nobel Laureate Rabindranath Tagore had sounded early warning bells about the destruction of forests.

Though Tagore was born in the city of Kolkata, he had a deep and abiding contact with nature from childhood, and it shaped his many-sided genius in diverse ways. As an adolescent, he accompanied his father Debendranath to the foothills of the Himalayas, an experience he wrote about in his autobiographical notes.

Later, he was a frequent visitor to a zamindari estate in Shilaidaha, now in Bangladesh, where many of his short stories and songs were written while on a boat on the mighty river Padma. He had experienced the vast expanse of nature – in the sky, in the mountains, in the rivers and the flat, verdant lands of the Bengal delta.

Simultaneously he witnessed the urbanisation of the sleepy villages around Kolkata and Kolkata itself, and lamented the oppressive bounds of concrete and the lessening of contact between human beings and nature. item.title: ‘Maxxing’ is just self-care and improvement repackaged for social media
item.description: Constantly focusing on how to maximise ourselves may inadvertently cause us to become more focused on what is wrong with us.
item.content:encoded:
If you want to improve yourself, your health or your lifestyle, you need to do it to the “maxx” – according to social media, at least.

If you want to better your appearance, you need to try “looksmaxxing”. If you want to fix your diet and look after your gut, you should be “fibremaxxing”. And if you want to improve your social skills and be more charming, you really ought to be “personality-maxxing”.

But all of this maxxing might not actually be a good way to motivate yourself into healthier habits. In fact, it may have the opposite effect – and may even cause stress.

The language of “maxxing” has roots in the gaming concept of “min-maxing”, in which players strategically maximise desirable attributes while minimising less useful ones to create the most effective in-game character. The concept then made it’s way to the mainstream, most notably through “looksmaxxing”: making focused, and sometimes extreme, efforts to maximise physical attractiveness.

The suffix has since been adapted in multiple health and wellbeing spaces. If there is an aspect of life that could be improved, it can probably be maxxed.

item.title: How a male Marathi theatre star defined the role of the perfect Hindu wife in the 20th century
item.description: Bal Gandharva’s star persona became a site where respectable Hindu femininity was produced and commodified.
item.content:encoded:
For much of the 20th century, the most admired wife in Marathi-speaking India was not a woman at all.

Bal Gandharva (1888–1967), a celebrated impersonator of Marathi sangeet natak (musical theatre), played devoted heroines with such conviction that film actresses well into the 1970s were trained to reproduce his mannerisms.

How did a man come to define middle-class femininity with such authority?

My recently published research traces Gandharva’s enactment of womanhood from the stage to the marketplace.

It reveals how his star persona became a site where respectable Hindu femininity was produced and commodified – a project that the theatre industry, emerging consumer culture and Hindu nationalist politics each exploited for their own ends.

Staging respectability

India’s pervasive caste system divides Hindus into distinct groups based on which caste they are born into, with certain castes regarded as “higher” than others.

Some of these “lower” castes are made up of hereditary performers: families with a lineage of performing arts. Historically, women from these communities were allowed – and sometimes expected – to perform and entertain.

But Marathi sangeet natak, which emerged in the mid-19th century, was a predominantly upper-caste and middle-class practice.

item.title: Eating pulses can be great for the body, suggests science

Lentils, beans and chickpeas have been feeding people for thousands of years. Lentils are among the world’s earliest cultivated crops, with archaeological evidence tracing them back to the beginnings of agriculture. Yet scientists are still learning what happens inside our bodies when we eat them.

A 2026 review of the research examined the evidence on pulses and their effects on the gut and metabolism. Pulses are the dried edible seeds of legume plants, including lentils, chickpeas, dried beans and dried peas. Legumes are the wider plant family and also include foods such as soya and fresh peas.

The researchers brought together evidence from human studies with laboratory and animal research. So what does the science suggest pulses actually do once we eat them?

1. They feed microbes in your gut

Pulses provide plant protein and fibre, along with carbohydrates that are not always completely broken down before they reach the large intestine.

There, gut microbes get involved. When some bacteria break down fibre and other carbohydrates, they produce substances called short-chain fatty acids. These help support the lining of the gut and are involved in how the immune system and metabolism work.

Gather all the footprints you’ve left thus far
on earth – be it in cafés, in cities, on bridges,
farthest continents, across the tidal dance
of a fable, beneath the felling gaze of a lover,
or within the duplicitous denials of dirt. Gather
them in a bag of jute, tied with a string of reed,
and release them into the ravening sea. Gather
all the footprints you’ve left thus far on earth

away, like mist. They’ll swirl, at first, then
tread the contours of a letter, before framing

the Buddhist name for Destiny.

item.title: ‘Fake claims’: Great Nicobar lighthouse project study lists species found in Africa, Amazon
item.description: More than 90% of the species in the tables in the environmental impact assessment study for the Indira Point plan have never been reported from Great Nicobar.
item.content:encoded:
Species primarily found in Africa and the Amazon have been listed in a recent environment impact assessment study claiming that they live on Great Nicobar Island.

The report released in April was prepared by WAPCOS Limited, a Gurgaon-based public sector undertaking as part of a proposal to repair the lighthouse and construct tourist facilities at Indira Point, the southern-most point of the island – and of India.

Tables in the environment impact assessment report list tiger fish (Hydrocynus vittatus), a native of African freshwater rivers, and the flagtail (Semaprochilodus insignis), an Amazonian freshwater fish.

Also listed are sambar (Cervus unicolor) and barking deer (Muntiacus muntjak), two species of mammals found primarily on India’s mainland.

More than 90% of the species listed in the tables in the study have never been reported from Great Nicobar. In many cases the closest sites are thousands of kilometres away.

Ecologists and marine biologists who have spent decades studying Great Nicobar said the report was “shocking” and alleged that it was “completely fabricated”.

The study includes the Eurasian woodcock (Scolopax rusticola), a bird of temperate and subarctic Eurasia that is found in Sri Lanka and along India’s western coast only in the non-breeding season, and the Mayabandar rice frog (Microhyla chakrapanii), which has only ever been reported from the Andaman Islands but not the Nicobar.

item.title: Microfinance promised economic freedom but created more debt for the poor
item.description: It was aimed at low-income households in Asian countries, including India, typically excluded from traditional banking.
item.content:encoded:
Microfinance was once celebrated as Asia’s tool to lift people out of poverty. From Bangladesh to India, Cambodia and the Philippines, the promise was simple: provide small loans to low-income households, help them start businesses, increase income and escape poverty.

Pioneered in the 1970s, microfinance was designed to provide financial services to low income people typically excluded from traditional banking.

Small loans, usually between US$200 and US$500 (about Rs 19,000- Rs 47,000 at current exchange rates) were particularly targeted at empowering women to start businesses and support their families. According to the World Bank, more than 1.7 billion people do not have access to banking.

Yet decades of experience suggest that credit alone has not delivered the transformation to economic independence promised.

We need to ask a difficult question: what if we solved the wrong problem?

Based on flawed assumptions

One fundamental problem is the assumption that poor households in developing nations lack capital but have profitable investment opportunities.

In reality, many poor families operate very small businesses such as food stalls, small shops, farming, tailoring or petty trading. These activities are often labour intensive and face intense local competition.

item.title: Amrita Pritam’s two Delhis: The city she lived in and the city she wrote
item.description: The writer was born on August 31, 1919, in Gujranwala, Punjab Province. She came to Delhi in 1947.

I have spent the better part of a decade reading and rereading Amrita Pritam in Punjabi, Hindi, and Urdu. Every once in a while, I translate her into English, as a way of staying close to her. Beyond the poem written on a train during Partition, the marriage she left, the half-smoked cigarettes of half-requited love, the 40 unwed years spent flouting mid-century convention, I have come to find two Delhis: the city she lived in and the city she wrote.

Pritam arrived in Delhi in 1947 and remained there until she died in it in 2005. She had a working relationship with the city – an announcer’s job, a daily commute, a house paid for, in effect, by 33 years of editorial labour – and a separate, far less forgiving relationship with it as a subject. An old black cat slept snugly in its chair in the Yunnan-themed, street-facing restaurant on Mae Salong’s main road. It was oblivious to the gentle exhortations of two middle-aged women, who asked it to make way for three hungry travellers, excited about the halal fare served there. Beneath a picture of the Kaaba, photos of tantalising soups, noodles, and salads were hung.

The food was not quite Thai, not quite Burmese, certainly Yunnan-inspired, yet very familiar to the three of us. The neighbouring shop played Chinese pop music, and the signs around us were written in English, Thai and Chinese. On the street outside the restaurant, two bystanders spoke in accented Thai, telling us the cat was not going to move, so we ought to find another table.

We had driven two hours from Chiang Dao in northern Thailand in search of tea, supposedly the Assamica variety, grown in the region since the 1980s. My Thai-Australian friends had been here before and they remembered the road being rougher than the smooth, tarred highway we were on.

I, on the other hand, kept marvelling at the landscape, which reminded me of Northeast India. “We could be driving anywhere between Nagaland and upper Assam, you know,” I repeated.

The reading of Chandu Maheria’s moving memoir, Homes Without Windows, translated into English by Hemang Ashwinkumar, must begin with the cover. It shows a photograph taken in a studio of two brothers, wearing uniforms but no shoes. The photographer had slipped ties around their necks, and Maheria, who still has the photo on his desk, marvels at their “dapper” selves. But the “unshod feet” tell the story of a life of extreme poverty, deprivation, disadvantage and exclusion that Maheria and his siblings struggled to leave behind.

It’s not an easy book to read, but Maheria fills it with wry humour that was perhaps, more than anything else, a coping mechanism. When friends asked why they hadn’t worn chappals, he quipped that the studio didn’t allow footwear. The irony is not lost on Maheria or his readers that he hails from the chamar community whose “hereditary occupation” is tanning and cobbling. There’s a poignant chapter, “Your Chappals, Our Skulls”, in which he recalls an incident when he was five or six years old, the year being 1964 or 1965. item.title: Gulzar made his name in Mumbai, but Punjab never left him
item.description: A short tour of Punjabiyat in Gulzar’s film song lyrics.
item.content:encoded:
Gulzar, named Sampooran Singh Kalra at birth, moved to Mumbai via Delhi at the age of 16 from Dina, a town in Jhelum district that is now in Pakistan. Punjab never quite left the multi-hyphenate genius, as is evident in his poetry, short stories and film song lyrics.

Gulzar recently marked his 92nd birthday. His fame rests on his reputation as a leading Urdu poet, alongside his contributions to short stories, screenplays and film song lyrics. His pen name itself means ‘garden’ in Urdu. But his Punjabi heritage survives in numerous ways. In fact, his early writings and film credits mention his name as ‘Gulzar Deenvi’, a tribute to his birthplace.

The recipient of the Gyanpith Award and the Sahitya Akademi fellowship, among other accolades, displays a rich Punjabi flavour in his writings. Gulzar’s family members were displaced from their ancestral home due to Partition. The sundering of the subcontinent is evident in the short story collection Ravi Paar as well as Footprints on Zero Line – Writings on Partition.

While Gulzar has been inspired by a variety of writers and poets, Rabindranath Tagore among them, his film song lyrics bear the unmistakable stamp of Punjabiyat, or the shared cultural identity among the communities of Punjab.

item.title: Cottage cheese: Do the protein claims add up?
item.description: There is relatively little research on the impact that cottage cheese has on muscle gain and weight loss.
item.content:encoded:
Cottage cheese is having a moment. It’s being added to dips, mixed into batters and even used in pizza and brownies. It’s touted as a high-protein food that can help build muscle and lose fat. But the research supporting these benefits is not quite as abundant as the number of viral cottage cheese recipes that are out there.

My colleagues and I published a review last year which provided a full breakdown of the available evidence.

Interestingly, our review did not identify any published studies which directly examined the effects of cottage cheese on muscle mass, growth and function. There were also no studies investigating whether eating cottage cheese leads to meaningful changes in body weight or body composition.

This means that much of the current hype around cottage cheese and its benefits is really only based on what we know about protein in general. There is actually relatively little research on the impact that cottage cheese has on muscle gain and weight loss.

item.title: ‘Timshel’ and goodness: What John Steinbeck (and ‘East of Eden’) can teach America in its 250th year
item.description: Steinbeck dreamt of an America that was not defined by ruthless power or an expansionist’s triumph, but by principles of empathy, justice, and dignity.
item.content:encoded:
The United States of America turned 250 this year amidst political upheaval, economic anxiety, and declining trust in institutions. This has left many Americans questioning the meaning of national-level experiments. At such a moment, I pondered over the writings of John Steinbeck, which felt surprisingly contemporary. More than half a century after his death, the author’s works still reflect upon the moral choices that confront the nation today.

In the words of his biographer, Jay Parini, “Steinbeck is one of the great writer-didacts, which means he was a perpetual student of humanity’s ways and means. Like Emerson, the founder of what critic Harold Bloom has called ‘the American religion’, Steinbeck ransacked the natural world for signs of immortality…He was, in Emerson’s great phrase, an instance of a Man thinking, a person whose thought was ongoing, exploratory, and always contingent, situated both temporally and spatially.” Steinbeck’s later writings, such as East of Eden, The Winter of Our Discontent, America and Americans, Travels with Charley: In Search of America, seem relevant, and this relevance prods the capacity to see his land as of promise and peril. He understood his nation as a moral process constantly negotiating between the American Dream and reality.

item.title: ‘The Struggle’: This impactful novel in translation presents a lived experience of agrarian unrest
item.description: Showkat Ali’s novel gets its emotional and narrative depth from how personal struggle is woven into the wider socio-political fabric.
item.content:encoded:
There’s an intensity to Bangladeshi writer Showkat Ali’s novel The Struggle (translated from the Bengali by V Ramaswamy and Mohiuddin Jahangir) that stayed with me well after I had finished it. Set in rural Bengal in the 1940s, the story doesn’t have any dramatic twists; instead, it builds through accumulations of hardship, small indignities, fleeting kindnesses, and most importantly, the will to endure. The result is a novel that feels both real and historically grounded without becoming didactic.

This story is about Phulmoti, a young widow navigating a world that is structured to box her in from all sides. Widowhood is not just a personal loss; it becomes a social condition that strips her of protection and rights and exposes her to scrutiny and exploitation. Her relationship with Qutubali, an unexpected ally, is one of the novel’s best parts. The novel as a whole resists easy sentimentality; what emerges is something more fragile and believable, shaped by circumstance rather than idealism.

“I will ask a news outlet in West Bengal to do political campaigns, political criticism,” Adhikari said at an event to mark the Hindu festival Raksha Bandhan. “But don’t attack saffron. The result will be terrible. You will not be able to handle the terrible consequences.”

Adhikari added: “Apologise within 24 hours. Print it on the first page…the writing was wrong. Otherwise, there will be a protest by those wearing saffron.”

item.title: Nepal flood: 10 bodies recovered from Gandak river in Uttar Pradesh
item.description: All the deceased were adults and believed to be Nepalis, the authorities said.
item.content:encoded:
Ten bodies have been recovered from the Gandak river in Uttar Pradesh’s Maharajganj and Kushinagar districts in the past two days following the flash flood in Nepal, The Indian Express reported on Saturday.

The Gandak, also known as the Narayani in Nepal, flows from Nepal into India before joining the Ganga.

The deceased are yet to be identified.

All the deceased were adults and believed to be Nepalis, The Indian Express quoted unidentified officials as saying. The bodies have been kept at mortuaries in Maharajganj and Kushinagar for 72 hours, they added.

“If no one comes forward during the 72-hour period, further action will be taken in accordance with government guidelines,” the newspaper quoted Maharajganj Additional District Magistrate Prashant Kumar as saying.

The Gandak also swept away several other objects, including vehicles, household items, gas cylinders, drums, furniture, logs and other debris, which have been washing up along its banks.

The toll in the flash flood and mudslide in Nepal increased to 616 on Saturday. More than 2,400 persons were missing, the country’s disaster management authority said.

More than 4,400 persons had been rescued, Prime Minister Balendra Shah said.

item.title: ‘My highest goal as an author is to make something seem incredibly, desperately real’: Meg Mason
item.description: An interview with the bestselling author of ‘Sorrow and Bliss’, whose latest novel, ‘Sophie, Standing There’ is about readers observing their favourite authors.
item.content:encoded:
Meg Mason is the author of the novels You Be Mother, Sorrow and Bliss, and, most recently, Sophie, Standing There, along with a motherhood memoir, Say It Again in a Nice Voice. A novel about bohemian parents, unemployment, the end of a marriage, and starting over at 40, Sorrow and Bliss was notable for its realistic portrayal of mental health and marriage and became a major international bestseller for that very reason. It was shortlisted for the 2020 Women’s Prize. Her first career was in journalism, beginning at The Times of London, later writing for Vogue, ELLE, GQ, Sunday Style and The New Yorker’s Daily Shouts.

Born in New Zealand, she now lives in Sydney, Australia.

In Sophie, Standing There, Mason takes the reader behind the scenes of literary stardom and anxiety. Sophie, freelance sound technician for literary festivals. She is a big reader and recently single. She hasn’t felt so lonely ever before in her life. But then, Sophie discovers Lilac Dunne, an author of great fame, through books, podcasts, and social media. She becomes obsessed – but it feels like love. There’s a slim chance of Lilac and Sophie crossing paths, despite their shared professional world. But what if they did?

item.content:encoded:
A special court has taken cognisance of the National Investigation Agency’s chargesheet in connection with the November 10 blast near Delhi’s Red Fort, ANI reported on Saturday.

This paves the way for judicial proceedings in the case to begin.

The NIA has named 13 persons in the chargesheet, including three who were named in a supplementary chargesheet.

The next hearing in the matter is scheduled for September 9.

The blast near the Red Fort metro station left at least 11 persons dead and several injured. Umar Un Nabi, a doctor, was believed to have been driving the car that exploded. Nabi died in the blast.

Two days after the explosion, the Union government described it as a “terrorist incident”.

In May, the agency filed its first chargesheet against 10 persons in the case. It alleged that all of them, including Nabi, were linked to Ansar Ghazwat-ul-Hind, which it had described as an offshoot of Al Qaida in the Indian Subcontinent.

The agency also alleged that the group aimed to overthrow the Indian government and impose Sharia, or Islamic law, in the country.

Ansar Ghazwat-ul-Hind was formed in Kashmir in 2017 when some militants broke away from Hizbul Mujahideen – the largest indigenous militant organisation in Kashmir – and claimed that they were affiliated to terror group Al Qaeda.

item.title: Kuchipudi has lost its theatrical soul. An 85-year-old guru is trying to bring it back
item.description: In Kuchipudi’s birthplace, Master Rattiah is passing on an old tradition that asks dancers to sing, recite poetry, deliver dialogue and inhabit characters.
item.content:encoded:
Master Rattiah reserves his sharpest rebuke for dance that chooses spectacle over rigour. “Decoration,” he said, with scathing contempt. At 85, he has earned the right to be exacting. Pasumarthi Rattiah Sarma – Master Rattiah to generations of dancers – is among the few remaining masters of the nearly extinct Yakshagana form of Kuchipudi that is a complex alloy of theatre, dance, music and poetics.

For Rattiah, Kuchipudi is not merely movement: the dancer must sing, recite poetry, deliver dialogue and inhabit a character. The form he learnt as a young man demanded all of this, as well as the stamina for punishing footwork and the control to make all that effort invisible.

“I want controlled energy like a spring, not force,” he said. “The face and body should at all times show lalityam (grace), no matter how much effort you put in. Remember that the landscape of Kuchipudi dance is never flat.”

This month, in recognition of his mastery, Rattiah was awarded the fellowship of the Sangeet Natak Akademi. It is an acknowledgement of a tradition that has changed dramatically in his lifetime.
